clue.text: In shock, this individual looks very pale

definitions.text: In shock, this individual looks very pale

blocks.note: surface reading: someone in a state of shock, drained of colour
setter's reading: a shock is a mass of hair, and very pale locks mark this person out

explanation.surface: A person who has had a nasty fright goes white as a sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: A shock is also a thick head of hair, and 'looks' hints at locks: the person is pale-haired, not pale-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: An ash blonde has hair of a very light, greyish fair shade, so their shock of hair is pale.

clue.text: Woman's name seen in Catalan addresses

indicators.note: something seen in a phrase is visible inside it, running across the word boundary

blocks.note: the end of Catalan joined to the start of addresses

explanation.surface: A girl's name turns up in speeches given in Catalan.
explanation.definitionFit: Alana is a female given name, so it is a woman's name.

clue.text: Advance warning: principal's on drink

blocks.note: a school principal is the head
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A tip-off that the headteacher has been drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'principal's on drink' means the head is placed on top of the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A heads-up is an informal term for a warning given beforehand.

clue.text: Lender studio's last used in Network and Jaws?

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of the word studio
something used in another thing is put inside it

blocks.note: final letter of studio
a local area network, abbreviated LAN
Jaws is the film about a great white shark

explanation.surface: A film financier backs a studio whose final releases were Network and Jaws.
explanation.walkthrough: Network and Jaws look like a pair of 1970s film titles; only Jaws is used that way, while Network is the computing kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A loan shark is a moneylender charging extortionate interest, a predatory kind of lender.

clue.text: Having hardly anything on or pretty pants?

blocks.note: first meaning: having little to do, being idle
second meaning: rather poor, since pants is British slang for rubbish

explanation.surface: Someone nearly naked, or wearing only some attractive underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'pants' means rubbish and 'pretty' means fairly, so 'pretty pants' is 'quite bad'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both idle, with little going on, and of poor quality, two separate idiomatic senses.

clue.text: Be afraid of losing female attention

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away from the word before

blocks.note: to fear is to be afraid
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: Someone dreads a woman no longer paying them any notice.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone your ear is to listen to them, so ear means attention.

clue.text: One up for getting picked up by a stranger?

definitions.text: One up for getting picked up by a stranger?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone keen on a pick-up by a stranger in a bar
setter's reading: the digit a hitchhiker sticks up to ask passing drivers for a lift

explanation.surface: Someone eager to be chatted up by a stranger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up for' suggests willingness and 'picked up' a romance; really it is a hitchhiker raising a digit to get a lift.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitchhikers hold out a raised thumb to signal for a lift from passing motorists.

clue.text: Around India, Brown initially overdid foreign language

indicators.note: around means the next word wraps round the letter for the code word
initially points to the first letter of the following word

blocks.note: tan is a light brown colour
India is I in the NATO alphabet
first letter of overdid

explanation.surface: A traveller in India got far too much sun.
explanation.walkthrough: Taino was the Arawakan language of the Caribbean islanders Columbus met.
explanation.definitionFit: Taino is an extinct Arawakan tongue of the Caribbean, so a language foreign to English speakers.

clue.text: Count in Barking displays affected charm

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nobleman living in the London district of Barking shows a smarmy manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking looks like the east London place name; it is slang for mad. Unction is gushing, insincere earnestness.
explanation.definitionFit: Unction in this sense is an excessive, ingratiating earnestness of manner, a put-on charm.

clue.text: Prohibit individual from coming to pub? I might!

definitions.note: the clue's speaker is the answer: a person who might bar someone from a pub

blocks.note: to bar is to prohibit
an individual is a person

explanation.surface: A landlord threatens to ban a troublemaker from the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the voice answering the question: who might ban someone from a pub? The person serving behind the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A barperson serves drinks in a pub and has the authority to ban unruly customers.

clue.text: A flipping angry soldier fixed in purpose

indicators.note: flipping turns the word for angry over so it reads backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
mad means angry
a soldier ant is a kind of ant

explanation.surface: A furious soldier is utterly determined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word qualifying angry; here it is the reversal signal. Soldier gives ANT, as soldier ants are a caste of ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant means unshakeable in resolve, refusing to be persuaded otherwise.

clue.text: One on the line with right trouble about royal

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
to ail is to trouble
ca is short for circa, about
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: Someone on the phone has a row about a member of the royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal but simply gives CA, circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A railcar is a self-propelled passenger carriage that runs on a railway line.

clue.text: Scottish gals pinching large bums in America

indicators.note: pinching means stealing, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: lass is a Scottish word for a girl
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Scottish girls squeezing big American backsides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' wants to mean nipping the bums, but it means stealing: the letter is taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English ass is the word for the buttocks, which the British call bums.

clue.text: Petrosian will need to play to find sponsor

indicators.note: to play is to move pieces around, as a chess player does

blocks.note: the surname of chess champion Tigran Petrosian, taken as letters

explanation.surface: The chess grandmaster Petrosian must play to win backing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tigran Petrosian was world chess champion in the 1960s, so 'play' fits the surface neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: To patronise is to act as a patron, giving financial support, which is what a sponsor does.

clue.text: Dealer that worked around noon in the West End?

indicators.note: worked means reshaped, as metal is worked into a new form
around means the reshaped letters go round the time of day

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A drug dealer did business at midday in central London.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's main theatre district.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatreland is the nickname for the cluster of theatres in London's West End.

clue.text: Jazz hit

blocks.note: first meaning: a fast style of jazz from the 1940s
second meaning: to strike or punch

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a jazz record that topped the charts.
explanation.definitionFit: Bebop, shortened to bop, is a jazz style, and to bop someone is to strike them.

clue.text: Chopper with built-in obsolescence?

blocks.note: surface reading: a cleaver, axe or helicopter designed to wear out
setter's reading: a child's first teeth are bound to fall out and be replaced

explanation.surface: A cheap axe or helicopter made to break down quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: Choppers is slang for teeth; a child's first set is designed to be lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk teeth are temporary by nature, shed in childhood to make way for adult ones.

clue.text: Teenagers gone out, so let's dance

indicators.note: gone out suggests letters scattered and out of their places

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Young people have gone out for the night, so they want to dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolescents are young people between childhood and adulthood, roughly the teenage years.

clue.text: One like Jesus around? Repent drunkenly, right?

indicators.note: drunkenly means staggering, so the letters lurch out of order

blocks.note: ca is short for circa, around
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A preacher urges a drunk to repent, like Jesus would.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a container signal but just gives CA, circa.
explanation.definitionFit: Jesus is traditionally said to have worked as a carpenter like Joseph, so a carpenter shares his trade.

clue.text: Might you say The Karate Kid or Star Wars?

definitions.text: Might you say The Karate Kid or Star Wars?

blocks.note: surface reading: a hugely successful film, a box-office smash
setter's reading: a karate fighter who smashes wooden blocks with bare hands

explanation.surface: A question about how to describe two famous films.
explanation.walkthrough: Star Wars was a box-office smash; the Karate Kid, as a martial artist, literally breaks blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: A blockbuster is a hugely successful film, and literally one who smashes blocks, as karate experts do.

clue.text: Men sitting with a conservative in chapel

blocks.note: OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
taken as written
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Soldiers sit beside a Tory politician during a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: OR, other ranks, is a common crossword way to clue men.
explanation.definitionFit: An oratory is a small chapel set aside for private prayer.

clue.text: Function that bans ecstasy is wrong

indicators.note: a function that bans something keeps it out, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: sine is a trigonometric function
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A party or gathering that forbids ecstasy is out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: Function suggests a social event, but here it is the maths sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A sin is a moral wrong, an act that breaks a religious or ethical rule.

clue.text: Unoriginal bit of script by toilet one's sat on hard

indicators.note: a bit of a word is just one of its letters, here the opening one

blocks.note: first letter of script
lav is short for lavatory
one is I, and the 's is is
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A scrap of a screenplay lies by the loo where someone sat down heavily.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one's 'sat on' hard means the I and IS sit above the H.
explanation.definitionFit: Slavish means copying closely without originality, as a slave follows orders.

clue.text: Daley Thompson often put his foot in it

definitions.text: Daley Thompson often put his foot in it

blocks.note: surface reading: a blunder, saying something tactless
setter's reading: an athlete literally putting his foot into his running footwear

explanation.surface: The famous athlete was prone to embarrassing gaffes.
explanation.walkthrough: Daley Thompson was Britain's Olympic decathlon champion in 1980 and 1984; the idiom for a gaffe is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiked athletics shoe is what a decathlete wears on the track, so he often slips a foot into one.

clue.text: Old model king picked up in city abroad

indicators.note: picked up in a down clue means lifted, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a model car or train is a toy
K is king in chess notation

explanation.surface: A vintage figure of a monarch bought in a foreign city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' wants to mean bought; it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Kyoto is a major Japanese city and former imperial capital, so a city abroad.

clue.text: Time soprano and earl use a rubber?

blocks.note: an era is a period of time
S is the abbreviation for soprano
E is the abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: A singer and a nobleman ask whether it is time for protection.
explanation.walkthrough: A rubber is the British word for an eraser.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase pencil marks is to rub them out, which is what using a rubber does.

clue.text: English soldiers on court could be up for it!

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
RE stands for the Royal Engineers
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: English soldiers on a tennis court might be keen for a game.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers, RE, are a corps of the British Army.
explanation.definitionFit: Erect means upright or standing up, so it can replace up.

clue.text: Smelly Ohio angler repelled old American

indicators.note: repelled means driven back, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: O is a standard abbreviation for the state of Ohio
rod is an old word for an angler
O is the abbreviation for old
US is short for American

explanation.surface: A stinky fisherman from Ohio disgusted an elderly American.
explanation.walkthrough: Repelled here means sent backwards, not disgusted.
explanation.definitionFit: Odorous means giving off a smell, so it is a synonym of smelly.

clue.text: Drop of Pils drunk by South African resort

indicators.note: a drop of a drink is a tiny amount, here a single opening letter
something drunk by another is swallowed into it

blocks.note: first letter of Pils
SA is the abbreviation for South African

explanation.surface: A South African swigs a little Pilsner lager at a holiday spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a resort town built around mineral springs.

clue.text: Straddling a good man, having intercourse

blocks.note: taken as written
ST is short for saint, a good man
ride is vulgar slang for sex

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of someone sitting on top of a decent fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Astride means with one leg on each side of something, which is straddling it.

clue.text: How are you with US tart? I'm disappointed!

blocks.note: hey is a casual greeting
ho is American slang for a prostitute

explanation.surface: A greeting to an American prostitute, then a sigh of letdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How are you' is a greeting, not a question to answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Heigh-ho is an exclamation of resignation or mild disappointment.

clue.text: Beer-covered duke gets rare dram in town

indicators.note: covered means wrapped by the word in front of it

blocks.note: ale is a type of beer
D is the abbreviation for duke
R is an abbreviation for rare
a dram is a shot of spirits

explanation.surface: A duke drenched in beer orders an unusual whisky in town.
explanation.walkthrough: Aldershot is a Hampshire garrison town, home of the British Army.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldershot is a town in Hampshire, England, so it fits the bare definition town.
